speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, July 4, 1977, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cullen that Bill C-27, an act to establish the Department of Employment and Immigration, the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission and the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, and to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof, be read the third time and do pass; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre).

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate a great deal has been said about the problem of unemployment. It has been very interesting to listen to people quote statistics on the large number of unemployed. If a person is unemployed, it does not really make much difference to him if all his neighbours are unemployed, or if there are a million people or a million and a half people unemployed in Canada. For him, unemployment means a total change in his standard of living and the way in which he relates to his community.
Many members are too young, and some have poor memories, but the remarks made last night by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) everyone in Canada should take very seriously. During the last depression, one afternoon a young fellow came to my father's farm and we hired him to help with the hay and milking. I remember his being paid $25 a month, which was probably $10 more than he would have had from a neighbour, since my father was fortunate enough to have a government job in 1935. When war was declared, I enlisted in the air force. I remember walking down one of the tunnels in the asylum for the insane at St. Thomas where they trained all the Commonwealth technicians for our war effort. I remember passing a guy and saying "Hi". Although this guy was a wing commander and I was an AC-2, he was the same man who had worked for us for $25 a month on the farm and was damned glad to get it.
[DOT] (mo)
I also remember others who, because they were veterans, were moved into northern Ontario and given land you could not have grown anything on if you had been the late J.C. They were put on that land as a favour because they were veterans. I remember one of these veterans in particular, my father-inlaw, who had been a successful businessman in Windsor and had moved to the farm at a time when you could not get enough food to feed the children. Yet in less than 10 years he was running the major employment branch of Hill-Clark and Francis, one of the largest woodworking factories in North America at that time, being responsible for about 400 employees.
It seems to me that we are doing the same sort of thing again. It is possible today to get a job digging ditches, if you want to dig ditches. You can get a job picking tobacco or tending to the crop before it is picked. It is possible to get a transient type of job. But we have a very highly skilled, highly trained and highly motivated group of young Canadians, many of them products of the baby boom following the last war, who are now looking for work. Although we made an effort to train them, they find it impossible now to get any employment. What a terrible waste. We have educated them to enter a society which is incapable of providing them with gainful employment.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said last night, we will end this before long by having a world confrontation, by having a war. This is all society is capable of doing. As sure as I am standing here, we have learned nothing in the last 50 years. We have already had two major wars to end unemployment, and it looks as if we will have another one very shortly. Such a war could break out anywhere. I am not a prophet and cannot pick the spot, but this time it will likely be in Africa.
It seems to me that after the last war we believed we were smart enough to be able to control our own society and economy and no longer would we have to settle unemployment problems by war, by killing off a few people and dumping production in the ocean or some place because there was not enough money to buy it. No longer should we talk about the Rothschilds or the Carnegies or other well known families which may have played a very large role so far as the last war is concerned. We should realize there were many economies which just did not have enough money in the system to make it possible to purchase the goods they were capable of producing. We are again in that position, not only so far as food supplies are concerned but other commodities as well.
I remember the very homey remarks of the late leader of the Social Credit party, Real Caouette. He used to talk on televi-

July 5, 1977
Employment and Immigration
sion about the need for sidewalks in a certain community. He pointed out that we had the people, that we obviously had the sand, cement and the water, and that we had the cement machines to make the cement. All we needed was the will to put it all together and we would have sidewalks. But if any of the ingredients are missing, whether it be the manpower, the water, the cement or the sand, it is pretty hard to make sidewalks.
Something is missing today, Mr. Speaker, since we are not able to build houses or to provide an adequate living for Canadians although this country has resources in abundance. But we will be able to do so if there is a war. If we get mad enough at somebody else, we will find a way. We will have the will, we will provide the money, and we will realize our immense potential.
Let me tell the House what happened at the beginning of the last war in regard to something we need very badly today. Canada has one of the longest coastlines in the world. There is an abundance of fish off our shores. We have some oil and gas off our shores. There is immense potential in the sea. We are a trading nation, and therefore we need the sea as a highway to move our goods to market. But we do not have any ships. The same was true at the beginning of the last war. We built the liberty ships and a merchant navy which grew to be third largest in the world. Then, right after the war, C.D. Howe sold it all to Onassis, and Onassis died a very wealthy man. So we learnt nothing from that; we still do not have any ships.

speechtext:
Perhaps I am taking a circuitous route, but I was trying to say that when we went to NATO they indicated that we would have to move supplies to Europe, and that most of them would have to be moved by boat. Surely, we and the rest of the country can see us having to hire a Panamanian, Liberian or Onassis fleet to take our goods from this country to the areas in need. The point I am making, for the information of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), is that there are measures we could take to end the unemploy-

ment problem in Canada, and if we do that the minister will not try to cut down the benefits which we pay to our unemployed.
It seems to me that the honorable member for Hamilton West has not been able to participate in this debate except to say, "Me, too. Yes, Mr. Minister, you have cut it down a little bit, so I will support it". That is no answer. The answer must be to provide employment so that jobs are made available for people in this country. I think it is damned important for us to put the problem in the right perspective; that is, we have the trained people and the resources in this country, yet we are still incapable of providing the jobs and the benefits that should flow from them. The production lost as a result of strikes has always been pointed out. Sure, we have strikes in this country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: A hell of a lot of them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
That may be true. But the loss in production as a result of unemployment is far greater than the loss in production as a result of strikes. Nobody ever talks about that. The hon. member who made the comment a while ago is a Liberal; therefore, he should be interested in a Liberal way in facing the problems of the country. That means providing employment and the government giving leadership. All the government is saying is that they cannot get the money, and therefore have to cut back on the benefits paid to the unemployed.
I said last night, in the few moments I had to speak, that no matter how good this minister may be, he is not capable of handling this department in the way proposed. Immigration is a major problem in this country. The province of Quebec is saying that they want a say in matters of immigration. So immigration is very important. But if it is so important, why do we tack it on to the tail end of the employment structure in the nation, when we have never had as many problems in that area as now? Surely, if the government were serious, it would break up this department, take immigration out of it, as well as some ancillary functions, and leave employment and unemployment to the minister who should be working in close co-operation with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour not only to provide benefits for the unemployed but also to provide jobs for them.
The minister refers to young people as bums, and to housewives as creating problems in short-term employment. I heard that when I was a kid. I heard that all the people walking up and down the road were bums. They were bums in the sense that they were hobos or gypsies travelling from place to place. Many young people know today that you can travel from coast to coast in this country and still be unable to find employment.
What is the government's answer? It is to reduce payments to those who are in the very worst circumstances. Let me say, for the benefit of the hon. member for Hamilton West who does not seem to understand this problem, that it is very much like the gun legislation. It depends to a great extent on where you come from and what your aspirations are. If you live in downtown Toronto, it is quite possible to visit 1,000 employers
July 5, 1977

in a month and ask for 1,000 jobs; but I suppose that 50 per cent of members here represent ridings with communities where there is only one industry. In such communities it is impossible to get a job unless someone leaves his job or dies. The only way to solve the problem in such cases-and it is a reasonably simple way of solving the unemployment problem-is to set up an additional industry. In my community there have been two major bankruptcies recently, resulting in the loss of about 1,000 jobs, which meant that approximately one-third of the whole labour force was affected.
Unless another one-third of the labour force leave their jobs, there is no possibility in the near future for the unemployed one-third who have been laid off, because of the bankruptcies, to find employment in that community. They can either leave the area or they can stay there and hope that someone, somewhere will be able to provide them with a job. Many of these people enjoy the dubious benefits of short-term assistance from the federal government, the dubious benefits of the Canada Youth Program or of Canada Works. These benefits are dubious because they are obviously only a stop-gap measure. They do not provide these people with training or allow them to get ahead in any chosen profession. They do not do anything but supply them with sufficient income to maintain themselves and their families for a short period of time.
I cannot help but think that if you were to give that kind of donation to a young businessman-in my area it amounts to about $200,000-he would probably set up a business which would employ 50 or 60 people, which would provide permanent jobs and which would be expansionary in nature, thus creating additional jobs in the future. The kinds of jobs that are provided in these types of programs are temporary, mundane jobs that do nothing for a person's morale or future opportunities.
Unemployment insurance has always been the scapegoat of the Liberal party. They have used unemployment insurance since the day it was proposed by Woodsworth to Mackenzie King. Mackenzie King did not only see it as a benefit for the people, but also a benefit for the Liberal party-and it certainly has been used as that. I remember when they brought into the program, for political reasons, the fishermen from the east coast. They had no chance of being employed year-round because they could only fish part of the year. The rest of the year they were subsidized by the unemployment insurance fund.
The next time there was an election, the bushworkers were brought in. They are seasonal workers in the forest industry. They became indicators in the systems. Every time there has been difficulty, unemployment insurance has been changed and tampered with. That is what is happening this time. The minister had no intention of going beyond 12 weeks until the hon. member for Hamilton West made a big fuss. That big fuss resulted in the minister's own backbenchers raising a hue and cry and demanding that those in less advantageous areas be given a temporary advantage. The scheme the government
Employment and Immigration

speechtext:
I am not questioning the Chair. I am suggesting that I am in order. If I reflected on the decision of the Chair in any way, I apologize and I withdraw those remarks. I felt that the hon. member for Hamilton West was not paying very much attention to what I was saying, or he would have known that I was in order at the time.
Perhaps some hon. members do not know the problems we already have with regard to the computer. Since it has been introduced, the computer has had to take into consideration a number of factors which are not necessarily related to the amount of the contributions or to the pay-out of benefits which takes place in the day to day operations of the act. In addition, there are other factors such as the national unemployment level as ascertained by Statistics Canada, Canada Manpower, and so forth. The national figure is a very dubious one, but it is inserted into the computer and that figure is used despite all the other factors involved. Now there is another factor. The regional factor will also be fed into the computer and each case will be calculated according to region. That is so complicated that nobody will know whether calculations are being done correctly or not.
Besides the 10 to 14-week requirement, there will be 54 independent areas. All this will be a nightmare for anyone trying to ascertain whether he is getting what he is entitled to. Also, appeals will be difficult. Instead of using all these complicated factors, it might be wise to go back to the system where claimants came face to face with the people who made the decisions with regard to claims. Rather than referring matters to district offices, or conducting appeals of various
7292

July 5, 1977
Employment and Immigration
kinds, including the involvement of members of parliament, would it not be much more simple for a person to make a claim face to face with the person who is going to make the decision?
Anyone who had anything to do with the changes which took place on at least two previous occasions will know that these latest changes will cause untold difficulty as far as the computer is concerned. In addition, the minister says we are going to apply this program over a period of three years, in varying degrees, and that at the end of the third year, unless parliament makes a change-and we can rest assured that it will make a change-we will go to the 14-week entrance requirement. Operating the system with a computer is going to be very confusing. Let me use an example so the minister will know what we are talking about. An unemployed person in Gaspe goes to Sarnia where there is a high employment rate. In Sarnia a person will have to work 14 weeks, and the rate will be different. Perhaps that person from Gaspe lives next door to someone from the local area. His benefits will have to be calculated in a totally different way than his neighbour's. There will be considerable difference in the length of time for which he will receive benefits. He will probably receive benefits when his neighbour will not be able to do so.
The minister shakes his head, but that is a fact. That is the way it will work. The minister wants mobility. That means people will be moving around the country. They will be moving from my area, where there is 15 per cent unemployment, to the constituency of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), where there may be a low rate of unemployment. People will be getting rates different from their neighbours'. Benefits will be calculated in a different manner. The length of time benefits can be received will be different in different areas, and the amount of benefits will also be calculated differently in different areas.
People in the department who have been involved with this subject for a long time are very good at changing one thing to solve another, but in doing so they often create about three new problems. The minister has to listen to them because this is complicated legislation and he has other problems to deal with which are just as complicated. Each person has an idea about how a particular problem can be solved. The minister seems willing to incorporate all this into the legislation. How much more simple it would be for us to discuss in this House the problem of how to create employment.
Surely, even the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling), who is making some noises, could give this parliament very good advice on how to provide employment. Indeed, most members of the House could offer ideas on how to provide full employment for this country. Surely, we are not going to wait until a general says that the only way to solve unemployment is to declare war, or a general somewhere else says, "For the good of the people, we will take the country over", as happened yesterday in Pakistan. And not only the generals, but the admirals. We had to get rid of one because I

understand he told the government that war is inevitable and we should prepare for it. He is right. War is as inevitable as the fact that the sun is going to set tonight and rise tomorrow-unless we can find a better economic system to provide employment for the people.
The war may take a very unusual turn because it may come from the people we have educated. They may bite the hand that fed them in the cradle because they have been trained in the stupid universities we have in this country. They are stupid; there is no doubt about that. We have business schools, but they cannot train people to start a business. Who starts a business in this country? The man who never went to college but who just got out and did it. The college man would not start a business because he has studied Adam Smith and knows the theory that it would not work today.
This stupid clause which will create a calamity for people in underprivileged areas of the country will pass because the government has the numbers-not because they are right. They have the numbers, and they have friends in other places to assist them. Surely, no one in this House would agree that changing the Unemployment Insurance Act is the best way to solve the problem. It can only be solved by providing work for the people now seeking unemployment insurance.
Not long ago I inquired at the Manpower centre in my town about the number of women in the area who were unemployed. Something like 150 women were registered for employment at that time. The manager of the office told me the same thing that the leader of my party has been saying for a long time, namely, that there are probably more hidden unemployed in this country than there are registered unemployed. He suggested that there might be 300 women looking for work, not just the 150 who were registered. When K-Mart opened a store in a shopping centre in the area, 300 people applied for employment in one day. I am told that altogether 1,200 people applied for the 75 part-time jobs paying the minimum wage. The government and the Conservatives say that people do not want to work, but these 1,200 people would have liked to try. Maybe they would not have liked the jobs, and maybe they would not have stayed. I cannot tell that. They did apply for employment, however, and employment was not available.
Mr. Speaker, I hope we send this bill back so that consideration can be given to this clause.

We realize, Mr. Speaker, that a war of attrition has been launched. The government has decided to stand pat. It was probably deceived by its officials, because we know that in the end they are the ones who do the work and direct the minister in his decisions. I think that at the outset the minister meant well, even if the bill gave rise to long discussions and several changes.

He brought in some minor changes to the bill after it had been considered at length in committee, he decided to rewrite the whole bill if necessary to bring in other changes: but I think what this bill needs is a radical overhaul. We are dealing with the superficial, and the civil servants-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that. You intervened a moment ago but other speakers before me have had more time. Of course, the Chair can always call members to order on this amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, an amendment dealing with clauses 29 and 30, but I think that if we are to understand this amendment to clauses 29 and 30 it is necessary to speak a little about the bill to see what brought on this discussion. It is all very well to restrict the debate without talking about the core of the matter.
The Chair wants us to try to pluck the bird without knowing specifically what kind of bird we are dealing with. Furthermore, I must say that I am not prepared to accept these matters of restrictions. I simply want to talk about the motions put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre providing some amendments because the minister tells us that he increased the qualifying period and reduced the benefit period. Then, he is telling us that those who will benefit most from the new system are the regions with a high unemployment rate. Let us see. Having cut down at both ends, the minister talks about the regions with the highest level of unemployment. So I am justified in fighting back because there is a 30 per cent unemployment rate in my area, Mr. Speaker.
I was furious when I heard people talking about 12 weeks, and rightly so. This was changed from 10 to 14 weeks but it is not yet in proportion with the unemployment rate in our area at all, Mr. Speaker, especially when the benefit period is reduced to 30 or 32 weeks. What is the result of these amendments? It means that the unemployment insurance fund will save more money and that the Liberal government will go on levying taxes as they have been doing for 15 years, while transferring the responsibility on to the provinces because after 30 or 32 weeks, the guy will not be able to get unemployment benefits and he will still be without work. Then he will fall under the responsibility of the province.
The Liberal government is so apt at shifting the responsibility on the provinces that we would not dare talk about it at the present time. Finally, however, the provinces will be forced to care for him through welfare. They will have to replace the federal government which has the funds, which taxed the workers for this unemployment insurance fund and now that they have been taxed to the hilt the government turns off the
Employment and Immigration
tap, keeps the funds and tells them to go to their provincial governments or to refer to welfare services in their province.
This is all we will end up with, in view of these amendments. And people are surprised. They say here that the efforts of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) to introduce the notion of regional disparities into our unemployment insurance scheme are far from gaining the support of all hon. members in the opposition, and I am sure that if hon. members on the government side could speak their mind and have their say, they would show that they are not happy about them either. They are not more stupid than we are, but they are not allowed to say what they want. They are simply sitting there, waiting for this war of attrition to end.
It is most unfortunate indeed to have a system of government which operates like this, for I feel that all together, we in this House certainly represent the larger number of Canadians and want them to obtain a fair deal and compensation for all the taxes they are paying, but that is not what is happening today. We need not wonder why none of the provinces are happy with the federal administration. None of them are happy because the federal government is getting too much for what it is willing to give back. The proof is right here, in the number of weeks and the arrangements for paying unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, in the beginning, I was rather pleased with this work because the idea was to reunite the two services, but I now realize that this reunification will double the number of public servants and that we shall have twice as many well-paid public servants while the unemployed will receive nothing, and that twice as many public servants will benefit from the taxes paid by the workers to protect themselves. Of course, the public servants are well protected! The trouble today is that we have a public service government. There is now one public servant for every four people; if we go on like this, tomorrow there will be one public servant for every two residents in Canada. Let us go on, everything is fine, but during that time, people are starving. It is a good thing that part of the population is working, but in a few years, I believe there will be more people out of work than people who are working, and that those who work will get discouraged and will put an end to this whole system because today, those who earn $400 a week give $175 in taxes to the federal government. This is what hurts and it is expensive. I therefore believe that we should draw the attention of the government to this subject. It is very well to say that wage increases are accepted, but I believe that the government accepts them because it is profitable.
We are now reducing the number of weeks to get rid of the high level of unemployed. There is one point that I would like to make. It is true that there are unemployed people with a good education, I admit this, but what have we done in this regard? I would like to give an example of the unemployment problem at the higher level. I now have a list of young people aged from 20 to 25, technicians who have a degree in electronics. Mr. Speaker, these technicians would like to work. The employer is there and is trying to give them work. He wants to

do so, but as soon as he is discovered, he would have to pay a $500 fine to the Quebec Construction Board, even though he would like to hire people who are much more competent than the old employees who got their trade card because of sympathy. Today, these young people are not directly under the jurisdiction of the federal government, but I believe that the federal government should, as much as possible, bring pressure to bear in this case because the situation is disastrous. These young people go to the Quebec Construction Board for a trade card. They have a trade. They have degrees. But the union leaders control the situation and the young people are told: We have enough people, we do not need to hire anyone else or still, you do not have any experience. They are told to go and gain experience when they cannot even get a working permit.
Mr. Speaker, I was using that example simply to indicate to the minister that that malaise exists. When he goes to discuss this with Quebec's manpower minister-I already suggested this on several occasions unsuccessfully-perhaps he will get better results. But it is a bad thing. And do not forget that those who have had the Quebec construction Board working permit for 25 or 30 years work six months a year and rest the other six. That is what I call unemployment with luxury. Those people earn $12, $13 or $14 an hour during six months, and then tell themselves they are going to pay everything in taxes, so they are better off not going to work. Those are the people on unemployment insurance.
Those are the kind of problems that need to be considered, Mr. Speaker. We must try to solve them to find the way to get ourselves out of that slump and allow our young people to enter the labour market before they decide to take the ultimate way out-revolution. I did say the ultimate way out because if you saw all the young people who come to my office you would realize that they are pretty close to revolution. When you consider that a young man cannot even get a simple labourer's working permit-I did say "a simple labourer's working permit"-without being fined! But when will we stop stifling people with all those fines left and right and telling people: You are not allowed to go here, you are not allowed to go there, you are not allowed to do that! Instead they are being told: Apply for social welfare. Mr. Speaker, as long as we will have bills like the one which is now before us, that will not solve the real problem. No. I call them public servants' bills to increase highly paid public servants and let the others starve.
I would like this discussion to end as soon as possible but I urge the government to act. It should be able to do something to bring about some changes in this area. We have come up with some suggestions and drawn its attention on these points. We are saying that the present work week is not consistent with the unemployment rates in our region or elsewhere. We should absolutely do our best to help those who are drawing unemployment benefits while working. That smacks of patronage! I believe we could reach a consensus by having officials draft omnibus bills, while government members are sitting still, waiting for the debate to come to an end.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I hope an effort will be made-for we are sensible people-to cut this debate short so we will not

have to spend the whole month of July in this House for nothing, while the minister keeps saying that he will not budge an inch. I am only asking the minister to think about it and make a final effort to bring this discussion to a close.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like some other members, it was not my intention to speak on this bill. However, in view of the economic situation in my constituency and the maritime region generally, I feel I have an obligation to my constituents and the people of that area to make this House realize that we are still a part of confederation even though the CBC on Dominion Day failed to realize it. Nevertheless, my remarks will be brief. They will be to the point and, in some cases, very pointed. The bill has some valid propositions. However, they are so veiled they do not appear as being valid. There are other points and questions in the bill that are questionable, particularly in view of the serious unemployment rate and the economic situation in this country, especially in my constituency and the maritime region generally.
Considering all the present circumstances, the economic situation and the unemployment situation, I suggest that the motion to have this bill set over for some months is proper. The bill should be considered, and the whole organization of the Manpower department, the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the allied bureaucracy related thereto should be considered. They should come up with something that is based on a positive policy of employment, which is a more positive and logical direction.
We should be talking about employment, not providing unemployment benefits. That is where the philosophy of this bill and its predecessors are wrong and out of place. The government should study unemployment insurance benefits, social assistance benefits, welfare benefits and welfare assistance in total and come up with a co-ordinated scheme to provide employment. Instead of unemployment, welfare and like social programs, we should be considering items like this. A special employment fund should be set up to provide for the carrying out of worth-while and necessary federally-funded and operated projects which would create employment in times of recession, depression and in slow growth areas such as the maritimes. In my own area of the maritime provinces, I speak of two items. I have spoken about these to other members of the House. I mentioned one that would provide employment and reduce the number of people on unemployment insurance.
As the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) stated, it is jobs that are important. 1 remind the government of the Chignecto Canal, a promise of confederation that has never been carried out. There have been 12 engineering studies paid for by the federal government, and three royal commissions. Not a sod of earth has been turned except the one by a member of parliament several years ago. Another project is Fundy tidal power. Why can that not be done? From an engineering point of view it is feasible. If projects like these
July 5, 1977

were carried out, those areas could get on their feet and be self sufficient. As well as providing improvements for the area, they would provide employment. We would not have to talk about unemployment insurance benefits.
We do not want to be a have-not area in the maritimes. I am sure the people in portions of Quebec feel the same way. If an employment fund were set up for projects such as those, to be built in times of economic depression and unemployment, people could be put to work. There would not be the same need for welfare, which is another matter. 1 will get to that later. If an employment fund for those types of projects were set up by the federal government, the cost of funding would be negligible. In addition to the improvements, the people in those areas would be paying income tax rather than collecting unemployment insurance benefits. Federal expenditures would negative one another in the long run. They would bring the maritime region and other slow growth areas up to the standard of the rest of the country.
I have a second suggestion. I put these suggestions in a very clear and helpful form in the hope that the government will do something about them. I listened to an American station. We get those down our way once in a while. Thank goodness we do, because the CBC does not do that hot a job. They tell me they do not have enough mobile equipment. The government should take steps to encourage and promote "workfare" instead of welfare. It should provide jobs and put people to work. There are many federal projects that could be started and completed during times of high unemployment.
There are good reasons for this motion. Items such as those mentioned could be considered during the layover period. A new bill could be prepared to provide those things that are logical, positive and sensible. If these suggestions were accepted, the bureaucratic population of Manpower, the Unemployment Insurance Commission and all the other allied departments under the minister could be reduced. Those public servants who would have to find other jobs would be more productive to themselves and to society in general. If projects such as I have mentioned were put into place, the whole system would be productive, people would be more productive and this country would not be in the economic doldrums in which it finds itself time after time.
The Chignecto Canal was a promise of confederation. I suggest it could be carried out if an employment fund were set up. I have brought this matter to the attention of the minister. He has been decent and fair. I hope he will discuss it with his cabinet colleagues. This is the type of thing that will create employment and provide long-term benefits for the whole maritime region. Like projects must be carried out in Quebec and other areas of slow growth. I hope the minister has listened to what I had to say and that his cabinet colleagues will take cognizance of what has been said here today.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not have an opportunity to speak on the principle of the bill on second reading. Nor did I have an opportunity to attend the committee meetings which went into depth with regard to the problems contained in Bill C-27. However, after hearing the hon.
Employment and Immigration
member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), who speaks in a very folksy and earthy way, talk about the problems confronting us as a result of unemployment and directly related to the Unemployment Insurance Act, I felt it incumbent upon me to say something.
The hon. member for Timiskaming, in relating the clauses that would be referred back by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for study, indicated that in his constituency a plant was intended to be opened. More than 300 women who otherwise would not have been looking for employment applied for employment. He stressed the principle that it is not only the 900,000 people who are unemployed at the moment; it is the number of hidden unemployed which is of major concern. Some economists have set that figure at between one million and V/i million. Therefore, it behooves all of us to direct our attention not only to Bill C-27 but to the larger question of employment.
I recall our leader speaking about a visit to Abbotsford, British Columbia-a beautiful province. In Abbotsford there was an employment notice to the effect that McDonald's hamburger chain was to open a new hamburger stand in the area. Believe it or not, there was a line-up a block long for people applying for the menial jobs which are related to the operation of a hamburger business. This underlines the situation we are facing.
It is rather striking that today we should be considering the question of national unity, the question of Quebec. We shall hear the leaders of all parties set forth their ideas on this subject. May I remind you, Mr. Speaker, that according to a survey carried out by the Toronto Star it is not the language issue which divides Quebec from the rest of Canada, but economic and employment issues. This is why it is so important we should tackle these aspects. According to the comments I read in the Star report, one of the sources of dissatisfaction in Quebec is that most of the English newspapers there are pussyfooting, wishy-washy and gutless.

speechtext:
Those are three adjectives which might well be applied by them to our Liberal friends in the government, and also to our Conservative friends. The main thrust of this bill deserves all those adjectives. One of the great things about debate in this House is that out of the clash of ideas comes wisdom. We started out with the idea that the minor attachment period would be increased from 8 weeks to 12 weeks.
I can still recall the opening speech of the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), the theme of which was: The Liberals have stolen our thunder. I recall the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp), the spokesman for the Tory party on manpower and immigration, saying-in Montreal, I think it was-that if he had his way, it would not be 8 weeks, 12 weeks or 14 weeks, but 20 weeks. So it was good to find the House engaged in a solid debate on second reading, because in the course of that debate we heard from members of the Liberal

July 5, 1977
Employment and Immigration party more representative of the maritime provinces and Quebec, and we also heard from members of the Conservative party summing up the reaction from their constituencies to the proposed changes. I am sure the members from the maritimes impressed on the minister the need for changes in the bill and were somewhat ashamed of the opening statements of the hon. member for Elamilton West and of the statements made by the hon. member for Provencher.
It is important that we debate this bill, and debate it thoroughly. I would not call the minister incompetent. 1 think he is competent, and I think he is sincere. I believe he is well aware of the difficulties. I have known him since 1968, and he has given me that impression. But he is caught within the web of the Liberal party and the cabinet, so his main endeavour is not to solve unemployment but to penalize the unemployed. This is unfortunate. I doubt whether he is deserving of the adjectives "wishy-washy" or "gutless", but he is caught in an unfortunate position. Coming from the city of Sarnia, he must be getting representations similar to those the rest of us are receiving with respect to unemployment.
Let me speak for a few moments about my experiences in my riding of Broadview, in Toronto, which I am sure is representative of a great many ridings across the country. It embraces many nationalities and economic groups; it is really a microcosm of the country at large. The main ethnic component is English, representing between 40 and 45 per cent of the population. When I first began to represent the riding, the figure was in the region of 65 per cent. Next in order of number come the Greeks and Macedonians, then the Chinese and the Italians. So the constituency is very representative of the country at large.
I operate a constituency clinic which I attend every Saturday morning. For weeks, months, years almost, I have not had people coming to me with the sole pre-occupation of finding employment. In the last six months there has been a dramatic change in my work at the constituency clinic. Every week five or six people ask me to help obtain employment for them. For my part, I do not believe a politican should be looked upon as one who obtains employment for persons. I believe he should be looked upon as one who is concerned with national issues and who directs his attention and resources to dealing with them. He should not be seeking employment for his constituents, especially since there are other agencies which have been set up to do so. The Department of Manpower and Immigration, for instance, is playing an effective role in this area.
As I say, five or six people come to my office every weekend seeking employment. Their ages range from 16 to 65, but the largest group is in the 16 to 25 age bracket. It is discouraging to find men in the prime of their working life telling me they have served in the armed forces, that they have worked hard, that they have been laid off, and that they have done their best to find employment but without success. It is disheartening to hear them tell me of their family responsibilities, their need to buy food, clothing, to keep up rent payments, and so on. It is equally disappointing to hear young people between the ages of 16 and 25, many of them with university education, telling me

they have looked for work and that employers have told them they are overqualified. In other words, all their years of study in high school and university counts for naught.
There are the semi-skilled and the unskilled. The government has attempted in some way to update the skills of many of these people, which is to its credit. Within the bill there are provisions for retraining and upgrading some of our workers. It is necessary to do so. These people are faced with a major worry; that is, having finished their courses and being retrained, there is no employment for them. This has a psychological impact on the way they apply themselves to their studies and skills. It has a tremendous impact, as well, on their general well-being if they cannot find employment.
On third reading, the minister's speech related directly to the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to refer back to committee for study clauses 29 and 30 of this bill. One of the objectives of the minister is to streamline and improve the unemployment insurance program in order to make it more responsive to economic circumstances. He said the unemployment insurance benefits structure will be simplified and made more equitable. Every time I receive a phone call from someone who has an unemployment insurance problem, I feel very uneasy because of the complexity of the act and its provisions. Usually I have to depend on my riding secretary to assist me with regard to these complexities.
The minister said he is going to make it more equitable, and he set forth a very complex scheme dividing Canada into 54 regions. He also referred to a formula which will be known as the variable entrance requirement. Depending on the region, that requirement will be from 10 weeks to 14 weeks. This is the government's response to the cries and howls of the members within its party, the members of the New Democratic Party and the maritime members of the Progressive Conservative party. That formula is not workable. It is neither fair nor equitable to the workers in the maritimes, in British Columbia, in Northern Ontario or in any area of Canada.
Originally, the bill was from 8 weeks to 12 weeks. Now the minister wants the change to be from 10 weeks to 14 weeks. Canada has a very mobile work force. There is the difficulty of a young person working for a period of time in the maritimes where unemployment is very high. If that person decides to better his position by coming to Ontario he will be faced with a 14-week requirement. That problem will be multiplied in the various areas across this country. Therefore, the New Democratic Party considers the changes are difficult to administer and are so unfair to workers that they are not worth supporting.
With regard to the riding of Broadview, when you have unemployment you are faced with racial tensions, which is a very bad thing. When you have full employment, there is an easing of those tensions and there is no ill-feeling among the different races and nationalities, as there is when they are competing for employment; there are tensions between the people who are working and those who are not working. Some
July 5, 1977

unacceptable adjectives are imposed upon the non-working by the working. This may be because of feelings of resentment, jealousy, or what have you. Therefore, it is very necessary to devise a program which is fair, reasonable and equitable in order to reduce racial tensions and also to reduce the tensions which exist between the working and non-working across this country.
When we had unemployment problems in the past, we faced that problem by having wars. Many members, most notably the hon. member for Timiskaming, enumerated some of the results of trying to solve the unemployment problem by having wars. Wars kill off the flower of our communities, the young men and women. This is one of the effects of trying to solve the unemployment situation by having wars. There is an attempt to solve unemployment by giving massive credits to corporations in the hope that these moneys will be used by the corporations to reduce the level of unemployment.
We have regional development programs, we have major tax concessions to corporations with regard to depreciation allowances and with regard to accelerated depreciation allowances, and we have programs to generate employment in depressed areas. The result of the regional development programs set forth by the minister of that department, who is a sincere, concerned and devoted Canadian, is an unemployment figure of 900,000 which was supplied by the Department of Manpower and Immigration. The more accurate figure is between one million and 1.5 million.
The government has to take a new approach with regard to unemployment if we are to reduce it from 8 per cent and 9 per cent to 3 per cent. The figure should be 3 per cent, because that would take care of the people who shift from one job to another. The Liberal government and the opposition parties as well have a duty to provide full employment. We can talk all we want about freedom of religion, speech and assembly, but we must talk about some of the things which are closer to all Canadians. 1 am referring to the right to work and full employment. Also, there is the right of a person to develop his highest potential. There is the right to medicare and decent housing. These are the rights we should be stressing. The right to education has been included. These are things we should be stressing. I imagine that foremost is the right to work.
When I read the minister's statement on third reading regarding development by the government of the work sharing principle, it seemed to me there had been a cop-out in regard to full employment in Canada. When we get these work sharing principles in place, Mr. Speaker, we will find there are many people still unemployed. Many of the tensions that 1 spoke of a few minutes ago will still exist, and this will not bring about a good result.
What we should be debating now is a bill having to do with full employment. The bill should include some of the measures the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Jones) put forward, as well as some of those put forward by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), the members of the New Democrat-
Employment and Immigration
ic Party, as well as some of our Liberal and Conservative friends-because full employment involves us all. The major concern in this country is employment, and we should be directing our minds to employment rather than to Bill C-27 which deals with unemployment.
When 1 come to think of it, Mr. Speaker, employment for even 10 to 14 weeks is a national disgrace. When the UI bill was first presented to the House, it was never the intention of the government of the day to speak of unemployment in terms of 900,000 people but, rather, in terms of only 3 per cent- workers in the work force changing from one job to another who needed interim help during that changeover period. Neither was it the intention of the government to speak of 10 to 14 weeks' employment in order to qualify for unemployment insurance. I think we should keep in mind that our goal should be full employment, and that the minimum unemployment rate should be 3 per cent.
If I may be a little folksy for a moment, I recall when Bryce Mackasey was minister of manpower and immigration in 1971 and we were dealing with the eight-week requirement. Most members had received a tremendous amount of mail from teachers across the country because they were not included within the UI provisions previous to that 1971 amendment. I, myself, and many others argued that they should be included since unemployment affects all areas of the economy. During the last few years teachers have had a hard time obtaining employment. Our universities and teaching colleges are still turning out teachers who are unable to find work owing to general economic conditions. It was, therefore, a good thing that Bryce Mackasey had the wisdom and the foresight to include the teaching profession within the provisions of the act. Some teachers are now reaping the benefit of the changes which we brought about in 1971. Unemployment affects all- university graduates, the semi-skilled and the unskilled. No one is left untouched by the scourge of unemployment.
We need government measures that will depart from the old methods of tax allowances and job training programs and move to job creating programs which will meet the immediate needs of the unemployed. I am sure the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) will have no difficulty directing his mind to some of the major work programs which are necessary across this country. I have just returned from a convention in Winnipeg where I heard about some of the concerns delegates had in their areas, such as lack of transportation, housing, shortage of recreational facilities, home insulation, and some of the specific matters mentioned by the hon. member for Moncton and others. It is not sufficient for the minister to talk of streamlining and improving the unemployment insurance program so as to make it more responsive to economic conditions. We do not need amendments to the UI bill; we need a major thrust toward creating direct employment throughout this country.
The minister spoke eloquently and with sincerity about improving the quality of employment-related services of the federal government for all Canadians. This is why we have been talking about integrating the UIC and Manpower and

July 5, 1977
Employment and Immigration
Immigration. It is very important that we have a direct handle on these particular departments. I am sure that from his brief experience within his ministry, the minister has become aware of the multiplicity of problems not only with the UIC but with Manpower and Immigration. I rather admire the minister's capacity to absorb all the stresses and strains in those three departments, because they are tremendous. But he could make it much easier both for himself and for most Canadians if he brought forward employment-creating measures which would help to eliminate the need for improvements in the field of unemployment insurance and in manpower and immigration.
Your Honour may have noticed, as I have, that many people now look upon immigration with a jaundiced eye. At one time immigration was regarded as a necessary step in the development of this country. When I think of the contribution made to the growth of this country by immigrants over the last 50 years-I include the contribution of my parents and, I am sure, the parents of most members here-it has been fantastic. However, we are now reaching the point where people are looking on immigration policies with suspicion and distrust. We are encountering major difficulties with the amendments to the immigration bill in committee, and I think the whole cause of this is unemployment. If we can solve unemployment, this would ease tensions in regard to immigration. We would continue to have a flow of people into this country of all races and nationalities who would contribute to and enjoy the benefits of the resources of this country, and not only among ourselves but with the world at large.
In closing, I ask the Minister of Manpower and Immigration to give full consideration to the motion to refer back, moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in order to review clauses 29 and 30 of the bill. I ask him to do so, not in the light only of improving the 10-week to 14-week formula, but to review it in the context of the larger problem of unemployment and to come back with measures to meet this problem. If he did that, he would receive the grateful thanks of all Canadians and the admiration and respect of members of the House, as well as their support.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment put forward by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to refer clauses 29 and 30 back to the Standing Committee on Manpower and Immigration. When we completed the study of Bill C-27 in committee, I took it upon myself to form a package of the minutes of the committee hearings on the bill and the second reading speeches, which I sent out to every premier in Canada and every major trade union in the country, asking them to look them over and to give me their opinions, because I thought that was the kind of job an effective opposition should do. The answers have started to come in, and I want to bring to the attention of the House the first response which I received today. It is very fortunate that it came in today. It was from Mr. Richard Hatfield, premier of the province of New Brunswick. He said:
Dear Mr. Rodriguez:
(Mr. Gilbert.]
Thank you for your letter of May 9 in which you invited our comments on Bill C-27. As you are no doubt aware, the province has already expressed its opposition to two key portions of the bill, and those have since been modified in response to overwhelming general objection. There are a number of other aspects of the bill which we view with some concern, so I have asked my officials to prepare a brief on these items.
He has done that and submitted to me his brief on what took place in committee. It is certainly an eye-opener. When I think of all the nabobs the government has at its disposal, all the so-called experts, we in this corner in the House are limited in terms of number and expertise; but surely, with some ingenuity, one could get the opinions of responsible people like the premier of New Brunswick. The comments that are made are rather revealing. They may have some application to what will be debated later today and tomorrow in the House. The first thing that the premier notes-I think it is very important and that the minister and members should be aware of it-is as follows:
It is characteristic of federal Manpower programs that their implementation or change has considerable impact on provincial programs. While the province appreciates that the federal authorities must change their priorities and programs in response to changing labour market conditions, it can only add to provincial frustration to be presented, without prior consultation, with a plethora of curtailments, terminations, initiations, and modifications in such program areas as unemployment insurance, vocational training, and job creation.
While it is true the bill presently before you is one concerning which there was prior notification to the province, there was no prior consultation-that is, there was monologue, but not dialogue.

He says, further:
As noted, we have voiced our concern about the most serious aspects of the bill and changes have been made. We do not feel, however, that these changes are yet totally adequate.
What is very important with respect to the minor attachment period or the qualifying period is what he says next:
To begin with, they are, and appear to be, ad hoc adjustments made in response to general opposition.
We have made that comment in the debate on this bill. First, the minister brought in Bill C-27 based on his comprehensive review on the unemployment insurance program, which moves the qualifying period from 8 weeks to 12 weeks. Apart from the shortcomings of the comprehensive review, which we pointed out extensively last night, the minister got a lot of flak from the backbenchers in his party. Suddenly he discovered light, like St. Paul on the way to Damascus. Suddenly he was struck, and discovered that there are regions in Canada where unemployment is much more serious than in others. This great enlightenment has come upon him suddenly. Do you know why it came? It came because of the threatened embarrassment by his backbenchers. Members from Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Quebec objected to some measures in the bill and threatened the minister with the embarrassment of their voting against this bill. As Mr. Hatfield pointed out, quite correctly, the minister came in with ad hoc amendments to the bill. Mr. Hatfield went on to say:
They do not form part of an integrated yet flexible over-all goal regarding UIC. Secondly, the time constraint on the amendments completely negates the advantage of tying benefit and entrance regulations to regional labour market condi-
July 5, 1977

tions. To suggest that the 14-week rule will apply across the board in three years is tantamount to saying that in three years no more consideration will be given to regional conditions. This is a position totally unacceptable to the province.
The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) was very gentle when he said the official opposition has been pussyfooting around. It has capitulated and broken faith with its colleagues from the eastern parts of this country. Here is Premier Hatfield pointing out very important opposition. But the Conservatives are quick to jump in and pat themselves on the back, such as in the bumbling performance the other night when the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) took all the credit for this monstrosity of a bill which is being perpetrated on the people of Canada. The hon. member knows full well that, under the bill, at the end of three years the qualifying period will be 14 weeks. Here is a Conservative premier pointing out the serious shortcomings of such a provision.
Will regional disparities disappear in three years, I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and members of the House? Nothing in the government's previous action or policies indicates to me that they intend to eliminate serious regional disparities in the country. They say, in the bill, that after three years regionality will no longer be a consideration. That is a condemnation of the minister's approach to this problem. What they brought in with this superimposition of 54 regions and the 10 weeks' to 14 weeks' sliding scale is just a measure to get them off the horns of a dilemma. It was to save the government the embarrassment of having its own backbenchers voting against it. I am glad that the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) just came in.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: I have been here all morning.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I was just reading a letter from his premier. The government was looking for a way to get off the horns of a dilemma, and the minister and his nabobs came up with an ad hoc approach. The premier's letter points out other problems he had with the committee minutes I sent him, and with Bill C-27 in the form it now is. Premier Hatfield does not share my political philosophy, but I certainly admire his honesty and sincerity. I think he is a genuine conservative and I admire that. He is genuine and he levels with people. I admire that, too. When we deal with other problems at third reading of this bill I will read other parts of Premier Hatfield's letter with respect to work sharing, and so forth.
With reference to the qualifying period, our motion to send this bill back to the committee is a wise move. The minister and his nabobs are now hearing very constructive debate and constructive propositions with respect to the most serious problem facing Canada at the moment, namely, unemployment. What good is it to wrap ourselves in the flag and say that we have one country, if we still have 1 'h million unemployed? We should be trying to serve the basic needs of our people. The hon. member for Broadview pointed out that the right to work is a very basic and fundamental right of every Canadian. That was also pointed out in the committee. Many
Employment and Immigration
groups and individuals came before the committee. I cannot think of a group which put the whole problem in a nutshell better than the United Auto Workers. Since the Conservatives are famous for quoting corporate sector briefs, I feel it is important that I quote what I consider to be an excellent synopsis of the whole question. I quote from the UAW brief as follows:
Our society is characterized by a lack of job security. Jobs are dependent on the ups and downs of the market and the decisions of corporations geared to profit-maximization. At present the rate of unemployment in Canada is at a rate higher than at any time since the great depression and even the government acknowledges it will continue to get worse. As of March, 1977, Canada has a higher unemployment rate than any other industrialized country. As quick as the government was to restrain our wages in October, 1975, in the name of a national emergency, no such crisis is apparently recognized by the government today.
We want jobs; we need jobs; the right to a job should be as basic as any civil rights (if not more so). The failure of the government and our social system to guarantee this right forces us to depend on unemployment insurance. The government, in Bill C-27, is attempting to further erode even this secondary right to unemployment insurance, and it offers as compensation for this certain reorganizational changes in the manpower programs.
That is one of the most excellent presentations we experienced in the committee's consideration of Bill C-27. There is no question that we have a problem in creating employment opportunities. There are certain policy directions this government must follow. There is work to be done. There are many job opportunities to be seized.
The other day I read about our trade relationship with Japan. In that study it was noted that 96 per cent of our exports to Japan are raw materials. On the other side of the trade picture, 95 per cent of our imports from Japan are manufactured products, primarily cars, cameras and electronic equipment. That, in a nutshell, is a microcosm of the problem. We have been allowed to develop a hinterland economy. Our people rip raw materials from the ground, cut trees down, and ship them out. In the area I represent, the predominant industry is mining. Our men and women take raw materials out of the ground. These raw materials are put into a semi-processed state-nickel pellets: we call them nickel matte. We ship those nickel pellets to Pittsburgh. Falconbridge ships its raw material to Norway.
We are badly in need of government policies which would make it uneconomic for resource companies to ship raw materials out of this country. There should be measures to encourage the processing of raw materials in Canada to finished products. There is no reason in the world why this government should permit a great country like Canada, with its fantastic resources, to be raped by multinational mining companies. Canada is not only being raped; it even pays mining companies to depreciate our resources. As our former leader, David Lewis, often used to say, there can be no rape if there is consent-and that is often what happens.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it one o'clock?

ALCAN PIPELINE-POSSIBILITY OF ENVIRONMENTAL AND ECONOMIC STUDY OF DEMPSTER PIPELINE

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister and it arises out of the report yesterday by the National Energy Board about the possible construction of the Alcan gas line and the fact that the Canadian gas will be brought up, if it ever is, along the Dempster highway, a proposal about which we know nothing in terms of economic costs or environmental conditions. Given that recommendation, is the Prime Minister asking for the preparation or development of a study of the implications of the Dempster pipeline on native rights, economic and capital costs, environment and so on, so that the information will be made available to the Canadian people and in particular to the cabinet before they reach a decision so we will not find that the Canadian gas is locked in forever?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It has to do with the terrible rip-off Canadian consumers have been subjected to over the last few years with regard to rusting of automobiles. I fully concur with the actions of the minister today in this regard. An authorized official of the National Research Council said yesterday that rustless cars could be built. He said, and I quote:
There are no technical limitations to the production of a vehicle which would be free from corrosive failure for its normal mechanical life.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the following questions will be answered today: 1,406, 2,335, 2,558, 2,779 and 2,792.

1.	Is DREE aware that the 1976 APEC report Industrial Incentives Programs in the Atlantic Region comments that "it is simply hard to believe that the region requires nearly 300 incentives programs"?
2.	Has DREE taken any initiative to (a) coordinate (b) prevent duplication among the programs and, if so (i) in what way (ii) which programs?
3.	Is DREE satisfied that there is adequate coordination among industrial incentive programs in the Atlantic region and, if not (a) for what reasons (b) which programs is DREE dissatisfied with?
4.	Is DREE involved in any regular meetings which seek to coordinate two or more of the incentive programs, and is there any formal mechanism through which administrators of each program are notified of changes in other programs?

The reply from the Department of Regional Economic Expansion is as follows: 1. DREE is aware of this statement but its own analysis suggests that the number of financial incentive programs in direct support of industrial development in the Atlantic region is but a fraction of the stated amount.
2.	As a matter of policy, DREE takes into consideration any assistance made available to applicants under the Regional Development Incentives Program by other departments, provincial governments, municipal or local bodies. This prevents duplication between programs and helps ensure that their application is coordinated. As a further coordination mechanism, larger and more complex cases are reviewed by the Incentives Advisory Board, composed of representatives of DREE and other federal departments.
3.	DREE believes that the policy and procedures outlined in the above answer to question 2 provide for an adequate level of coordination with other programs available in the Atlantic region.
4.	DREE is involved in regular meetings with officials of the federal Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce to coordinate the application of the Program for the Advancement of Industrial Technology (PAIT), the Program to Enhance Productivity (PEP), and the Industrial Design Assistance Program with the application of the Regional Development Incentives Act (RDIA). Through such arrangements DREE is kept informed of any changes in the provisions of these programs.
