No, Mr. Speaker, they are not, and I can go into the details of the new equalization formula. As a result of the decision reached in the new fiscal arrangements, there is in excess of a $1 billion net increase to the province of Ontario over any other province. On behalf of my party, I want to say that the kind of Canada we want to build is not one in which we will find the rich provinces, whether Ontario, British Columbia or Alberta, becoming richer at the expense of all the rest. We will have nothing to do with that.
Hear, hear!

Quite apart from any notion of equality which, from my perspective, is so central to the argument, I appeal to my colleagues in the other parties to consider the following argument. If they are not interested in principle, in the notion of equality as such, I would ask them to think about the implications for national unity. If this kind of transfer continues, whether in the tax system or constitutionally, what it will mean is that the Atlantic provinces will build up a set of grievances against Ontario and against British Columbia, and perhaps Saskatchewan, after a few years of bad crops-and that is possible-will find itself once again in a have-not position. This will cause great resentment against the richer provinces. By giving more power to the provinces, either in the form of constitutional change or fiscal transfers, what we will be doing is sowing the seeds of future discontent in our land. So for national unity reasons alone I think we should oppose this kind of move.
July 5, 1977

If we reject that kind of constitutional approach seriously put forward, what is the option? Do we revert to the kind of centralized federalism that we have had over the last ten years, one that has shown no respect for or sympathy with the nationalist development in the province of Quebec; one that has insisted upon a rigid application of national programs, whether we are talking about hospitalization or CMHC, right across the land? 1 suggest that is not the option. There is a third alternative, and I should like to sketch in what I think some of the components of that third option are in terms of Canadian federalism at this point in our history.
First, we want to emphasize the need for an effective national government with a national program, whether we are talking about unemployment insurance, medicare, hospitalization or housing. All of these programs must be maintained on a national basis in order to give Canadians from coast to coast some reason to identify with the national government. Such programs can be nation building.
Second, we suggest that the government take the rhetoric of decentralization seriously, but instead of decentralizing fiscal power or constitutional power what they should do is decentralize in a fundamental way the administration of such programs. They can establish housing programs on a very broad scale and money will go to the provinces to build homes within a certain income category and price range, but then leave to the provinces the right to decide what kind of housing they will build. We do not need the rigidity that we find in CMHC.
Hear, hear!

The housing needs of New Brunswick are different from those in downtown Vancouver, and both, again, are different from those in rural Quebec. So let us turn over pretty completely the administration of such national programs to the provinces, the same as 1 said on another occasion in terms of hospitalization. If the provinces are to get money for hospitals, they should not be told, as the government has told them in the past, to spend it all on acute care hospitals. Maybe one province needs more nursing homes than acute care hospitals. Again, the solution is not to get rid of such national programs, which I take to be the logic of the Conservative party. The solution is to maintain such programs, but to radically decentralize the administration and give the provinces the right to decide whether it makes more sense for them to build acute care hospitals or nursing homes. That is our second point, that we can have substantial decentralization in the administration of national programs.
The third point I would make, particularly at this point in history, is that we need a massive program to deal with unemployment. The Prime Minister recently came back, with what I took to be some kind of pride, from a meeting of seven industrialized countries and said that we are not unique, that all countries have the unemployment problem. What he did not point out is that among the seven countries we are the worst. He casually forgot to say that the other six have an
National Unity
unemployment problem, that is true, but two or three of them have social democratic governments which are doing a hell of a lot better than Canada is with the combination of inflation and unemployment. That is the point. Certain governments are prepared to involve themselves in the kind of national economic planning that is necessary to deal with both inflation and unemployment, and the resolution passed by my party on the weekend calls for such a national planning effort on behalf of this government.
Fourth, I turn to the constitution. It is our view that some constitutional change is necessary; some is inevitable. There has been change in the past and there will be change in the future. Some sensible proposals have been made by a number of Canadians both inside and outside this House, but I want to stress that in our view the basic structure of our constitution is sound and the prime source of our current tensions and problems in Canada does not come from the constitutional structure we now have. It comes, rather, from the policies and leadership, or lack of leadership, in the politics associated with that constitution.
I suggest that, for example, in the province of Quebec where the cultural problem is the serious one, Rene Levesque is showing that within the present constitution the French language can be made the language of work for the people of Quebec-and I and my colleagues, salute and support that effort. Second, the effort to make changes in the distribution of power in the province of Quebec can be done within the present constitution. It is the case that the minority of Anglophones dominates the power structure in the corporations in that province, and it is the case that if the prime minister of that province wants to change that, as he does, he can do so within the present constitution and we should encourage him in so acting.
Finally, another aspect of concern to the people of Quebec, as expressed by a good number of them, anyway, is that they want to get more control over their natural resources, as do a lot of people in other provinces who support the philosophy of my party. I say through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Premier of Quebec that if he wants to do to the asbestos industry in Quebec what Alan Blakeney has done in his province to the potash industry, more power to him. He can do that also-I want to stress this-within the existing constitution.
Hear, hear!

Although we are very open, as a party, to those who want to propose constitutional change, it is certainly our view at this point that that is not the primary concern and that more basic economic and cultural matters and problems can be solved by political and economic decision-making within the present framework.
Let me conclude with our last point. What I think is really required in our country, more than anything else, is a leadership which says to the people of Quebec and to ordinary Canadians outside the province that there are, in fact, two great cultures. I say that to the Prime Minister who tries to pretend that somehow it is simply a multicultural society. It is

What we require, surely, from the national leadership is for those of us who are federalists to say to the people of Quebec, "Let us work together. There is an immense amount of good that we can do. Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Social Credit Party of Canada, I am pleased to take part in this important debate on national unity, or more especially as far as Social Crediters in the House are concerned, on the constitutional future of Canada. The conditions in this country have changed substantially in 110 years. We have evolved from a mainly agricultural and stable society into an industrial, technological, urbanized and active community in the business world, so that our needs have also changed.
Some clauses of our constitution should not have been altered, while others should have been abolished or slightly amended. Considering our present constitutional document, the Social Crediters are demanding a new constitution for several reasons and among others because our constitution is already 110 years old. It was not drafted in Canada, by Canadians, for Canadians without outside pressure. And then our constitution is still in London after 110 years and we are not sure where it is localized and how it could be patriated. With this so-called Canadian Constitution which no longer meets our needs and which causes us so much trouble to patriate, it is the contention of the Social Crediters that it is easier and better to have it where it is, especially when we consider the trouble its patriation would entail in relation to its real value in Canada nowadays.
A new constitution drawn up by the provinces is the safest way to come up with Canadian constitutional harmony, to the satisfaction of all parties involved, namely the provinces. We should not be unduly bothered Mr. Speaker, by the constitutional troubles Canada experiences at this time as we are contemplating a new constitution. France and the United States have set up their constitution in more dramatic circumstances than ours, following bloody revolutions. However, the procrastination demonstrated by this government, as well as previous ones, and its attitude towards the provinces in the present constitutional crisis could only lead us, perhaps too soon, unfortunately to a situation which other countries have experienced with regret.
Sentimentally, the Social Crediters identify themselves with the whole country. Intellectually, 1 am sure that the future of everyone will be better if we stay together. Why should we separate or divorce if it is to get married again. Thus I approve and we approve the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) not to

believe in divorce between the provinces or in the separation of Canada, nor in the marriage of the provinces under a so-called sovereignty-association. Still I cannot understand the actions of our Prime Minister in the light of what he says, for the actions of an individual generally reflect the actions of the country, and all the more so when one is Prime Minister.
Divorce and separation are totally contrary to marriage and national unity. On December 3, 1976, 1 made a speech in the House on the value of the British North America Act of 1867, in the course of a debate on the constitutional issue which was initiated by the Social Credit Party after the Quebec election of November 15. I will not repeat today the arguments I put forward in that speech. However I would like to resume the discussion on this question by addressing myself to the new Canadian constitution which we have been claiming for such a long time, as I indicated in my speech of December 3, 1976.
In La Presse of May 4, 1977, Mr. Pierre Desmarais II, president of the Conseil du patronat du Quebec is reported as saying:
We need a refurbished federalism which the provinces have to redefine.
Mr. Speaker, we in the federal government think of ourselves as being all-powerful, those who have the absolute power. We in the federal government have to be the ones to tell the provinces what their constitutional future is. Well, here is what Mr. Pierre Desmarais II, president of the Conseil du patronat du Quebec, has to say:
Mr. Pierre Desmarais is in favour of a refurbished and renewed federalism which the provinces have to redefine.
Speaking before the Rotary Club and the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Metropolitan Quebec, Mr. Desmarais contended that one of the first rules of the game of Canadian federalism is "that the distribution of sovereign powers be consistent with the will of the provinces".
It rests with the provinces that make up the country to decide what part of their sovereignty will be shared with the central authority. The review of our constitution and the reorganization of constitutional jurisdictions are essentially the responsibility of the provinces. If they want to reduce their aggregate powers to increase their respective power the decision is theirs alone. There is no national will without the will of the constituent parts.
I think this is very important. I go on quoting:
There is no national will without the will of the constituent parts. This is the price we have to pay for our national unity.
To this extension of provincial responsibilities, Mr. Desmarais adds the necessity of proportional representation of French-speaking people at every level of the federal administration as well as the respect for the linguistic rights of the minority groups. However, he refused to elaborate on the form this division of powers should take, believing that it is for the provinces to sit at the table and determine what they expect from the federal system.
In response to the terms of the conference entitled "Why choose Canada?", Mr. Desmarais expressed his conviction that the federal system is the best formula to ensure the future of French-speaking Canadians because it is a flexible formula, because our institutions are able to adjust according to our needs and hopes, because it allows a combination of forces and because it brings men together.
In 1963, Mr. Speaker, addressing the Quebec Kiwanis Club, the Hon. Daniel Johnson, the late Quebec premier, stated as follows:
July 5, 1977

Before starting to draw up a new constitution, tailored to fit the needs of modern day Canada, the principle must be laid to rest according to which in a federal or confederal regime all provinces must of necessity be shaped in the same constitutional mold, have the same rights, the same responsibilities and the same sources of revenue. He added that a new constitution, perfectly adapted to the legitimate aspirations of the two cultural communities, would be possible only when English Canada and French Canada will have understood that Quebec is not, and can never be, a province like the others. Mr. Speaker, constitutions are made to serve man and not to enslave him. The greater and stronger governments become, the greater the risk of people becoming isolated from the main centres of decision. The 110 years of massacre inflicted upon the constitution of 1867 by the present government and its predecessors has led to Canada finding itself, in 1977, in a worse situation than it was in 1867.
Ever increasing centralization on the part of the federal government has provoked a back lash on the part of the provinces which clamour increasingly for greater autonomy. From that state of affairs stem two contrary political forces which have led Canada to the brink of the abyss of separation. Everyone knows that our so-called constitution of 1867 was never approved by referendum in Canada in 1865. Why weren't the people consulted in 1865-on a question of such tremendous importance, in which its future was at stake? This consultation did not take place because the debate was so hot at the time of Confederation that the bishop of Trois-Rivieres, among other people, had to intervene to calm down people and because the federal government of the time feared being beaten in Quebec by a referendum; so they decided to avoid the verdict of public opinion by having their plan approved by members only.
A new confederation should comprise autonomous communities with equal rights, but in no way subordinated to one another, although united by common allegiance, namely the principle of equality of all provinces in a new constitution which does not mean that there is unanimous consent on the part of all members of the collectivity. A new Canadian constitution should give to the provinces the right to decide for themselves whether they want to remain in Confederation. This right would contribute to a large extent to prevent potential violence because of the right of peoples to determine their own destiny in peace and order.
All obstacles put in the way of promoting and abetting separatism can only accelerate what we dread. A new constitution should provide for flexibility, openness of mind, mechanisms for regular consultations between the federal government and the provinces and a decentralized federal authority which would supplement and strengthen provincial governments. Strong provinces would thus attenuate regional conflicts. It is thus essential to redistribute powers among more viable units. If the provinces see fit to reduce their present eleven parliaments and two territories, they should be free to do so themselves.
National Unity
An autocratic government can only appeal to a dictator. In a democracy, the government must look after the ordinary citizen, see to his welfare, his security and his expectations. It must consider his desires which are expressed through popular organizations and action committees within parishes. Government of the people, by the people, and for the people is infinitely more complicated than are absolute monarchy and dictatorship, for example. A new Canadian constitution as proposed by the Social Crediters would allow every province to determine itself its political and financial course in a Canada whose wealth and diversity could very well go with a decentralized federalism at the service of the provinces and not out to subdue them.
National unity might be a noble and desirable aspiration if it applies to English Canada only, but it becomes an irritant and against nature if it seeks to encompass French Canada. French Canada can only let itself be drawn into that national unity movement by sacrificing its own national characteristics and resigning itself to fusion and simulation. A single uniformity might be desirable in a country where there is only one nation, only one community, only one language and only one culture. We are against the Liberals' or this government's national unity because we are against the present constitutional melting pot.
We are against the status quo of this government. We are for national harmony via a new constitution because national unity in Canada, Mr. Speaker, is impossible since we have not one but two national communities. The province of Quebec must bear alone the responsibility for the French-Canadian culture. When the powers are uneven, the legislative and fiscal powers cannot be the same. It is wrong to think that all provinces must have exactly the same powers and the same means of action. It is in the name of that faulty principle that Ottawa continues to multiply constitutional subsidies for joint programs in provincial fields without leaving Quebec any other choice than conforming to common standards to recover the money it pays in federal taxes or tax itself again for the maintenance of its own institutions. What I just said, Mr. Speaker, with respect to the province of Quebec also applies to all other provinces of Canada.
It is in the name of this false principle that this government, this status quo government, is asking us to disregard the pact of 1867 in order to comply with the will of the majority in a federation where French-speaking Canadians make up 30 per cent of the population but control only one government out of 11. So long as the same constitutional straitjacket is imposed on all ten provinces, we will never get out of the present constitutional impasse. The two communities making up the Canadian nation will be a problem for each other.
The counterpart of this constitutional dead end lies entirely and solely in the sharing of powers among governments. If Canada exists today and if it is to exist tomorrow, it is on one essential condition, to remain a federal state in fact and not only in name. The federal state is a creature of the provinces. It seems this fact has been forgotten here. Its only purpose is to promote their common interests, that is the interests that

July 5, 1977
National Unity
the provinces feel are similar enough to be looked after by a sole representative for all, namely the federal government, for more flexibility, for the sake of economy or for greater efficiency.
The federal government must have limited powers. They should not have any other powers than those conferred upon them by the Constitution. They should not try to interfere with the responsibilities and jurisdictions of the provinces, neither in time of war nor indirectly nor under the pretence of their international role. They cannot either act through statements and on strictly political grounds, without first submitting the matter to the provinces, nor through fiscal means or judgments rendered by their own courts, nor can they do it in case of emergencies or for the protection of so-called national interests. They cannot argue either that evolution has traditionally been a centralizing force or that economic progress commands it or finally, that nowadays science and technology require greater centralization.
However, that is what the federal government has been doing in Canada for several decades. To cope with this situation, to counteract this centralizing trend, to avoid the disruption of Canada and so that the provinces are not reduced to mere administrative ridings and are in a position to assume their responsibilities for the better-being of their citizens and to avoid that French-Canadians are forever second-class citizens in their own country and, finally, to assert the principle of equality among individuals and groups, it is therefore essential that the new Canadian Constitution should provide for safeguards and limited federal powers.
These vital safeguards are the following: First, a constitution written in a clear language which cannot be subject to whimsical interpretation; a constitutional court whose fairness and non-partisanship would be unquestioned; a list of federal powers which would be limited with corresponding restricted fiscal powers; a compulsory constitutional amending formula which would not enable the federal government to unilaterally increase its powers.
These requirements are not met at present and in all fairness it can be said that this is the root of our political, constitutional, economic and social difficulties. Here is the answer: the provinces should be granted real powers. Having said that, I want to deal for a few moments with the suggestions made by the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) who advocates more centralized powers but an administration at the provincial level. This is nonsense because how could a province properly look after its own administration if the federal government retains all financial authority? How could a province decide upon the quality of housing if the federal government does not grant enough funds to build good houses in the provinces? Centralization has proved its worth in Canada. Since 1867, we have had ever-increasing centralization. Let us see what the situation is now.
Mr. Speaker, let us give real authority to the provinces! All the authority not conferred on the federal government by the initial constitution or by amendments thereto should belong to the provinces. This is the spirit of the confederative act, the

autonomy of the provinces or the self-determination of the provinces is the right of privilege and the ability to make one's own decisions. This right is the basis of the natural freedoms that are nowadays called "human or civic freedoms or rights" and also "political, economical and social rights". These rights are individual rights and no democratic state has the authority to take them away; it can only control and regulate them and prevent some abuse against others.
Democracy is founded on the autonomy and freedom of citizens; it also exists in the autonomy of the provinces. In very large countries, and I consider that Canada is one of the largest countries in the world, this autonomy, this freedom is handed down through regional institutions. This is why true federalism means that the provinces which make up confederation have the right to self-determination and to enter contractual relationships with one another through a constitution which must provide for the protection of their rights as provinces by keeping the peace among them, by maintaining law and order and preserving the traditions of each of them and by increasing the common prosperity.
Among all the federated states of the world-and there are more than 20-Canada is the only one where the federal government assumes full powers, and since this is against the nature of things, this issue should be clearly resolved, otherwise we shall never get out of the constitutional status quo in which the Prime Minister and the present government have put us. If, under a new constitution, full powers belong to the constituent provinces, it is useless to list them. Our constitution, like the constitution of the United States, should proclaim unequivocally that the member provinces are the founding provinces and that the founded state is the federal state. This brings me to give the following explanation: Only the constituent provinces can agree to amendments to the constitution. The federal state could never make such changes alone, neither through foreign legislation in London or elsewhere nor by a simple federal legislation. If at times there were matters on which provinces would not necessarily agree and the interest of several provinces would prompt them to accept an extension of federal duties, such extention could only be made through a constitutional amendment under a majority rule still to be determined. The constituent provinces would never agree to an amending formula unless they knew first what powers they are prepared to hand over to the federal government, but particularly as basic conditions: that they have full powers, that a constitutional tribunal be set up and that the constitution restrict the unilateral action of the federal state.
One of the most serious deficiencies of the present constitution is that it does not provide for an amending formula. The provinces cannot initiate amendment procedures. Moreover, there is no distinction between matters of major and minor importance and lastly, a constitution must be flexible, that is it must be easily adapted to the circumstances. This could be done by drawing up a list of possible concurrent powers, where the federal state can legislate and spend public moneys. However, the provinces could always act concurrently if they
July 5, 1977

wished. But their legislation should always have priority over federal legislation in all cases not otherwise provided for.
This does not mean, however, that the federal government would be excluded of all new activity. On the contrary, its concurrent powers should be more extended than they are now, but along with an opting out right without any financial or other penalty for those provinces which would not accept the federal paramountcy in the areas not clearly allocated to the federal government under the constitution. Such a sensible approach is to be found in every modern constitution. We are also convinced that the French language will never be protected by other than the founding province of Quebec. We are also convinced that the old federal parties are committed to centralizing residual powers in Ottawa, and that such a centralization effort stems from an electioneering approach on the one hand and the bureaucratic and financial establishment on the other.
In this light, the Social Credit Party of Canada is recommending a new constitution that would respect the principles stated earlier and allow for constitutional harmony between our Canadian provinces. Concretely the Social Credit Party of Canada urges the drafting of a new constitution made in Canada by Canadians for Canadians, aimed mainly at reviving the true Confederation spirit where the parties involved, provinces in other words, will recover and assume all the powers that belong to them, in order to protect and safeguard their identities and ensure their true participation in monetary, fiscal and trade decisions in Canada. In order also that such decisions taken at the federal level exert exclusive control on and deeply influence provincial economies and provincial initiatives.
The steps leading to a new constitution would therefore be the following: provinces will be responsible for establishing the constituent assembly to draft a constitutional proposal. The constituent assembly could be comprised of representatives of the people especially elected for that purpose, members of parliament and provincial legislatures, representatives elected by various organizations, with the help of experts in an advisory capacity only. The constituent assembly could hold sittings in every province, consult with all existing organizations, in order to be in a position to develop a modern draft meeting with the aspirations of every social class and the various groups.
Once the proposed constitution had been drafted, the various provincial legislative assemblies would scrutinize, amend and accept in principle the proposed constitution, which would then be submitted to a constitutional conference of all Canadian provinces. The proposed constitution would further be submitted to the people of each and every province through a referendum. Finally, this new constitution would become law on the date set in the constitution. It would give provinces complete responsibility with full powers, and extend to the federal level responsibilities to execute the mandate given by provinces for their greater social, economic, political and cultural development.

Mr. Speaker, as a Canadian who feels deeply and passionately about the future of this great country,
I deem it a great honour to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. I begin from the premise that Canada, after the election of November 15, can never be the same again. It seems to me we have two clear options. First, that we shall go on to be a stronger, more united country, more united than ever before; or, second, that-as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said earlier-we shall drift into separation by attrition and shall end up with French only being spoken in French Canada and English only spoken in English Canada. At times I see great hope for a stronger, more united country. At other times I am very concerned in case that which none of us wants should come about.
It seems to me that we are discussing, in this debate, the sorts of questions which arise in the discussion of any personal relationship. In any relationship, be it that of business partners or any other personal relationship, it is important for both partners to lay their differences on the table openly and frankly. If there are differences, one must ask if both partners are prepared to make attitudinal changes which will restore the former relationship. If that were not possible, I should be most concerned about the future of our great country.
Several have already spoken in this debate. Writers have written articles on the question and perhaps expressed their views more clearly than I can express mine. They have written articles about this country, studied its history and expounded the difficulties it faces with great clarity and depth. However,
I have made it my business, as a member of parliament, to travel across Canada and to participate in many different areas in the debate on national unity. It seems to me, therefore, that we are debating a fundamental question. When we debate the French-English question, we are really debating the right of a people to preserve a culture as old as this country. We must accept that a substantial number of our people are unilingual and their ancestry goes back to the beginning of this country. Also, when we debate this question we are debating equality of opportunity in education, economics and social matters. Perhaps, most important, we are debating the right of Canadians to be perceived by other Canadians as equals.
It seems to me that the debate has centred mainly on the French-English language question, but I should like to broaden this debate and put on record certain facts affecting the region of the country I represent. Mr. Speaker, I represent many people who came to this country in the last 20 or 25 years. Many of them voice the same concerns. Many of them belong to visible minority groups. They question their role in Confederation and whether they are perceived by others as being equal to other Canadians. It seems to me, no matter if we debate economic development in the maritimes, problems in the west, the aspirations of native peoples in the north to have their land claims settled, and objectives heeded by the rest of Canada, that the basic question with which we must deal is the

right of individuals to play a role in this country, a role equal to that played by other Canadians socially and economically. Our individuals seek these rights.
Perhaps I can draw an analogy with the anti-inflation program. Since the days when inflation was running rampant, it seems to me one can see a perceptible change in the attitude of many in this country. People were striving for almost unrealistic gains, were doing so with an attitude detrimental to groups not as strong as the ones to which they belonged. I think of business groups which made a point of saying that unions should be done away with. I also think of unions which said that what happened in future did not matter; they were concerned about present wage gains. An individual somehow felt in his position he was a good deal better off than the next person.
There is a whole harsh attitude, particularly in that part of Canada that I represent, toward people who speak a different language, have a different colour of skin, dress differently or come from a different economic stratum. It is all of these we should be concerned about. If we look at it in sheer isolation, we are not effectively speaking to the problems facing Canadians today.
I was attracted to a comment, reported in Maclean's magazine, by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Salts-man), and I quote:
We are in danger of becoming a nation of well off bitchers-province against province-group against group-region against region-person against person.
As a country we can only be successful if the larger, stronger, and more powerful groups are more charitable to the minorities and conscious of their rights and aspirations.
It all comes back to the question of attitudes and whether people are prepared to change and understand. I think they are and I think they can be. Who would have thought in October, 1975, when we had such a confrontation in our economy, that today business, labour, and government would be sitting down at the same table, perhaps not in total agreement but at least discussing some of the problems? If we can accomplish that, in spite of the threat of inflation presented to the country at that time, surely we should have a similar ability as Canadians to have that same attitude of wanting to look sincerely at the problems of national unity and seeing what we might be able to do.
I want to talk for a few minutes on what I think are some of the solutions to the national unity question and what the role of members of parliament should be in this entire matter.
I feel very strongly that we, as a government, have to stand four-square for minority rights. I am pleased that in this session of parliament Bill C-25 with regard to human rights and the discrimination question has been passed. The recent publication "National Understanding" was a large step forward for this. However, we do not want to leave it there in terms of having printed this policy paper and having passed that type of legislation. Everyone in this place has to believe
[Mr. Milne.)
sincerely the motivation behind that legislation and that document.
If we are not concerned enough to want to stand up for the rights of minority groups, not only to preserve them but to promote them, we will fail our country. Surely the many different viewpoints put forward by various groups relate to their concerns about this.
When we talk about the French-English question, this means that French speaking Canadians across Canada must have the types of rights that English speaking people want to have for English speaking people in Quebec. On that there are many points you can make. I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister comment earlier today about the tragedy at the present time of retrenchment on that in one part of the country rather than turning the argument around so that we are all concerned about bringing the rest of the country up to where it should be. It is not too late to rally to that side of the argument.
There is considerable danger that if we want to decide that very little can be done we will lose the advances that we have made in terms of minority language and other rights over the years. We have to support that side of the argument which maintains that the parts of Canada which do not offer real opportunity for minority language groups should do something about it.
I represent an area in Ontario, one of the richer provinces, one that could well afford to do a good deal more than they have been doing. I am desperately concerned that they get on with the job. If my knowledge of history is correct, in certain parts of Canada both official languages have been in the court system for as many years as this country is old. In some parts of Ontario today we find the situation where they are trying, on an experimental basis, to use both official languages. These are areas where there are substantial numbers of Francophones. This is something that has to be accelerated very quickly.
One of the difficulties that people in English Canada do not seem to understand and must learn to accept is that French has to be the working language in Quebec. Many of the people I talk to in English Canada somehow feel that this a real retreat from some other position. I refer them to speeches which the Prime Minister has made a number of times. It is as natural for many people in Quebec to speak French as it is for us in English Canada to speak English. Having said that, I am equally concerned that the freedom of choice for minority groups in Quebec be protected.
It does not seem to be very well understood in English Canada that for a very long time it has been possible for an Anglophone in Quebec to be born an Anglophone, educated as an Anglophone, work as an Anglophone, operate socially as an Anglophone, and die as an Anglophone. At the same time there have been full services in the provincial government over all these years in both languages. English Canada must now look very carefully, certainly where there are groups significant in number, at providing these types of services as well.

That is the kind of objective we should be working toward, rather than moving away from that position.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock, when we took recess, I was talking about some of the thrusts which I thought important toward improving the relationship between the English fact and the French fact, and suggested that this question should really be considered in a wider range.
One of the things I think is terribly important is the role the Francophone has played in middle and senior management in many companies in Quebec and, indeed, in the government here and across Canada. I think it has been well documented, and perhaps the record should show, that of 104 of the largest businesses in the province of Quebec, fully 90 of them are considered to be completely Anglophone, 43 of them did not have one single Francophone on their executive payroll, 23 of them had one, 13 had two, six had three, two had four, and only four had five or more. Anyone should be able to imagine from those figure how discouraged Francophones must be in the business community that their progress had not been more substantial than that.
The chief point I want to make in the remaining few minutes I have at my disposal is that whichever way this argument about the future of Canada turns out it will surely in the final analysis be determined through the political fact. The time will come when Canadians will have to decide whether the leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal party are best suited to handle this problem, or whether it is the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) or one of the other parties. Based on the speeches given today and the performance since November 15, no question remains in my mind about which person Canadians will vote for and follow. The Prime Minister has consistently gone across this country and talked about national unity. He has expressed the same point of view wherever he has spoken, and has garnered substantial support for this viewpoint on the matter.

It happens I have the floor at the moment and wish to put that on record. When you look at leadership, the
National Unity
leadership given by the Prime Minister has been outstanding. But my greatest concern is that Canadians might join the party called "Apathy", which would be the greatest tragedy of all.
I recently read a survey indicating that if the "undecideds" were left out about 28 per cent of the people in Quebec would probably be committed one way or the other to the separatist option. Perhaps about 40 per cent are committed to the federalist option, and another 32 per cent are classified as moderates. This argument will certainly be won or lost in the appeals to the hearts and minds of these moderates. There are many comments we could make on that, but in an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail on Friday, December 31, the Rabbi of the Holy Blossom Temple, Dr. Plaut, wrote:
Everyone agrees that there is a significant segment of Quebeckers, anglophones and relative newcomers as well as an important section of the francophone community who will remain deaf to the sirens of independence. Obviously their support is essential and they need to be strengthened, but their effectiveness will be limited by their numbers.
There is, however, a third segment. Its members are as yet undecided francophones whose votes will determine the fate of the province and of Canada. What can we do to attract them to the vision of one Canada? The answer will not so much lie in concession, handouts and credits, for most of them are not likely to arrive at this most important decision of their lives on the basis of short-run economic advantages. I think they can be swayed by new attitudes in anglo-Canada, attitudes which have been sadly lacking in large portions of the population. What they need to know is that they are understood and accepted in their differentness, and welcomed by a change of heart, and not merely with bilingual arrangements.
I would be difficult to say it any better than that.
I am watching the clock and see I have very little time left in which to speak. I wish I had the time in which to comment on the educational system. I am deeply distressed that the funding which is available is not being used by the provinces. Indeed in the riding from which I come a group of parents have been paying extra to have their children educated in French, and even then it has become a matter of concern as to whether that can be continued. Fortunately a decision has been made that it can continue, but I make the point that a lot of parents and a lot of constituents are way ahead of governments in terms of their desire to see secondary education in the other official language.
I also hold the view that the teaching of Canadian history in our schools is one of the most overlooked factors in this whole equation. I well remember in school hearing at great length about Hannibal taking the elephants over the Alps, but I would think there are many people in Canada who have only a very limited knowledge of the history of their country. Many students have looked on history as a subject to "get through on" whereas in fact it is extremely important to national unity.
In conclusion I should like to read into the record a letter I received just this morning from a person who had lived in Ontario and moved some three years ago to Montreal. He is now in the process of moving back to Ontario, and these moves are occasioned by the fact that he works for a company which has production facilities in both provinces. He says:
I'm sure you, like myself, are very concerned about our country at this time in its history. Living here in Quebec I can see major economic problems growing

day by day that have been brought on to a great degree by the events of November 15 last. In many respects these economic problems are bound to spill over provincial borders and have a profound effect on Canada as a whole.
The majority of the people of Quebec, as best I can determine, are not in favour of secession from Confederation. However, they are determined to bring an end to the second-class citizen status placed upon them by the majority of Canadians. To this end they have improved their quality of education and are today turning out science and commerce graduates that are capable of standing shoulder to shoulder with any Anglophone Canadian graduate from across the country.
The Francophone Canadian is a very proud individual. He is a different person than his parents and grandparents. He harbours desires for success and the amenities of life the same as all of us and is prepared to make the sacrifices to achieve them. His only reservation is that he wants to do it in his language of thought and not be compelled to carry on a full time translation process in order to get his point across.
I can sympathize with this desire as could any Anglophone who would take the opportunity to live for a period of time in Quebec. Language however has been at the root of many problems in the history of the world and possibly because we are such a young country we must make our own mistakes.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, nine years after the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) formed his first administration, almost eight months after a separatist government is elected to office in the province of Quebec, members of the House of Commons are finally accorded a two day debate on national unity. For this debate the government presents a resolution in which members are asked to dedicate themselves anew to the continuing unity of Canada. Some of us, indeed the majority of us, dedicate ourselves anew to this country each day we enter this Chamber. We do not need a prolonged debate to do that, but two days is pitifully short to explore the reasons for the deep divisions and conflicts in this country, and to put forward proposals as to how they can be met and resolved.
The resolution itself reveals a very simplistic approach to the issue of national unity. Since last November 15 we have been exhorted, or we have exhorted others, to stand up and proclaim how much we love our country. But words, however fervently spoken, are no longer enough. The Canadian people have passed through that phase since November 15. Yes, we can all be and are missionaries in the cause of national unity, as the Prime Minister urged this afternoon. But surely it is not necessary for any of us in this Chamber to reiterate our feelings about Canada. We know how deeply we feel, and through our actions we try to show it with every passing day.
What this country does not need, and does not want, is a Charles de Gaulle approach. It would be an affront to Canada, to Canada's history and to Canada's people, for any individual to try to pass himself off as the incarnation of the country or the saviour of the country.
The Prime Minister has said again and again that will and determination will carry us through. But will and determination, unless channelled into some meaningful forum, cannot in themselves resolve the crisis this country faces today. Canadi-

ans are looking for a forum, an agenda, or a plan of action in which they can participate on a continuing basis in this emergency. But they do not have such a forum because the people's representatives-the duly elected members of parliament-do not have such a forum, except for a limited two day debate on a resolution couched in platitudes.
The Canadian people are entitled through their elected representatives to participate in deciding what form their future will take, and surely the best framework for this task is a parliamentary committee, as my leader has proposed. The failure of the Prime Minister to recognize this fundamental truth makes me wonder if he would not deliberately reject this idea for his own personal aggrandizement. He was asked last April to establish a special parliamentary committee to deal with the problems in our federal system. He said he would discuss the suggestion with the government House leader. The House leaders subsequently did discuss such a move, and I can only surmise that the reason a special parliamentary committee on national unity is not being proposed by the government at this time is that the Prime Minister vetoed it.
Civic-minded groups all across the country are setting up committees to discuss ways to rectify the country's current malaise. Can the House of Commons, the most representative forum of the people, do less than that?
Let us take a look at what the government has done in these last few months since the election of a separatist government in Quebec. Faced with the most serious challenge to Confederation in our history, members of the government did what they do with any other problem. They created a new secretariat in the bureaucracy. They realized there was something very special about this problem, so they appointed two secretariats. The secretariats have swung into action collecting newspaper clippings, running Pequiste economic pronouncements through a computer and, of course, co-ordinating each other's work. Their multicoloured flow charts, their computers, their analyses-everything is in perpetual motion inputting to Canada's very first programmed Prime Minister.
Today we have the appointment of a special blue ribbon commission. As worth-while as the operations of that group might be, it is yet one further example of the contempt the Prime Minister has for the relevancy of this institution. For parliament to take this lying down would surely be the ultimate abdication of its responsibility. These are eminent Canadians whom the government proposes to appoint; but they do not have the mandate that we have as members of parliament, the one institution chosen by all Canadians. The challenge that faces parliament in this year 1977 is not one that can be delegated to any outside commission, no matter how eminent.
The Prime Minister might just learn something from history. I ask him to cast his mind back to the difficulties of 1864, when the union of Upper and Lower Canada ran into grave problems. It was all too evident that the system was not working. Did the political leaders of that day send for an architect of an earlier time to help devise a remedy? Had the
July 5, 1977

present Prime Minister been there, his answer would obviously have been to reactivate Lord Durham.
Hear, hear!

No, the political leaders of that day turned instead to their colleagues in other jurisdictions, to the working politicians of the time-Macdonald, Brown, Cartier, Galt, Langevin, Tilley, Tupper-and even though it took them three years of study, scrapping, reconciliation, and accommodation, they came up with a plan for a united Canada. They did not pretend to have the last word on Confederation. They were not searching for an ultimate truth, either to find one or to impose one.
The resolution before us and the attitude of the government for nine years suggest that language and language policy are the ultimate truth, that the country is defined by its languages, that bilingualism is the soul of Canada. This displays a very limited, a very narrow concept of Canada. Canada is much more than that. We know, Mr. Speaker, that economic disparities between English and French speaking groups, or between different regions of the country, exacerbate the problems of national unity every day they remain unresolved. But there is another dimension to the problem of national unity which has been largely ignored, and that is the political dimension. 1 do not mean by that the calling of an early election to capitalize on a crisis and thereby heighten the cynicism which abounds in the country regarding our political institutions. No, Mr. Speaker; when I refer to the neglect of the political dimension of this crisis I am referring to a long overdue analysis of our political system, our federal system, to see how it has to be changed to meet the demands of a greatly changed society from that of 110 years ago.
Over a century of experience in the art of federalism has provided Canadians with a workable political structure which is the envy of many countries throughout the world, given our complexities and diversities. But that does not mean that it does not require a major overhaul from time to time.
The agenda, the mandate, for a parliamentary committee looking into the causes of disunity in this country could cover a number of problems not presently being dealt with in any other forum in this House. It could monitor what the government is doing at the federal-provincial level and suggest ways to avoid the absurdity of one branch of government spending months working out complex new fiscal arrangements with the provinces, in complete isolation from another branch of government working on a language policy which, if implemented, would necessarily involve tremendous additional federal funding.
A special committee dealing with the problems of national unity might be able to bring some order out of this chaos. When lapses of that nature occur, is it any wonder the central government is regarded with distrust and hostility as the "alien they" by individuals, groups, and provincial governments across the country?
National Unity
Well, how to overcome this lack of legitimacy, how to bring a new harmony to the federal system, how to make our national institutions reflect the regional nature of the country which has forced the provinces to be the primary spokesmen of regional needs? These questions would be high on the list of priorities for a parliamentary committee to examine when considering the faltering political dimension of our federal system.
Another agenda item for this Commons committee could be the consideration of a regional base for certain of our national institutions. Provincial nominees on such major bodies as the Senate and the Supreme Court of Canada would be an obvious starting place. In addition the committee could examine the composition of the ever-growing number of regulatory, administrative, and quasi-judicial agencies which exercise such broad powers.
As Professor John Meisel of Queen's University puts it in a forthcoming paper:
Some of these agencies like the CRTC and the CTC are within federal jurisdiction but deal with matters vital to provincial development; others like the National Energy Board operate in areas where the provinces share constitutional responsibility. In both cases there are good reasons for shaping the structure and membership so as to provide closer ties to provincial governments.
I am gravely disturbed when I see major recommendations being made by a three man federally appointed board, such as the National Energy Board, in a field in which the provinces have unquestioned rights, and yet the provinces must come before board hearings in the manner of suppliants, with exactly the same status accorded to any individual citizen in this country. Is it any wonder we do not have a national energy policy when the main national agency for formulating that policy does not reflect the true political dimensions of the federal system? The same can be said regarding the lack of a national transportation policy, a national communications policy, a national regional development policy, etc.
But if regional or provincial representation were included in national institutions, Professor Meisel considers that "federal institutions would thus act as brokers of distinct regional and ethnic interests, and the decisions of such bodies, while applicable nationally, would result from the reconciliation of various provincial interests. Federal policies would more likely respond to regional interests, and also the regional interests represented in Ottawa would begin to perceive the national dimensions to their concerns."
The need to restructure the political-and by that I mean the federal-dimension of these bodies would be an important agenda item for a parliamentary committee seeking to eradicate some of the causes of friction in our federal system. Such a committee, if bold enough, might even examine the failure of this Chamber and of political parties to provide adequate national representation. On many occasions I have said that I believe the lack of strength of the Conservative party in Quebec over a long period of time, and the lack of Liberal representation on the prairies, have aggravated the threat to national unity.
